content: The World Health Organization (WHO) requested declarations of interest from all members involved in the evidence-synthesis teams, the guideline development group, and external reviewers who were invited to assess the recommendations during the guideline development process. This process was overseen by the WHO steering group in strict adherence to the WHO conflict-of-interest policy. During the guideline meeting, each member verbally disclosed any potential conflicts of interest and presented any actions previously communicated following the conflict-of-interest analysis. None of the members of the guideline development group reported any conflicts of interest. The guideline was developed in response to a public health emergency using a rapid-advice framework. The WHO steering group will continue to monitor research developments in the area of infant feeding, particularly in the context of the Zika virus outbreak. The group plans to reconvene within six months of the guideline's publication to review new data and determine whether an update is warranted. If an update is deemed necessary or if concerns arise regarding the validity of the guideline, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the update following the formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The guideline addresses the question of whether breastfeeding (either exclusive or partial) by a lactating woman infected with the Zika virus, compared to not breastfeeding, results in the transmission of the virus to the infant or young child. The population of interest includes women who are breastfeeding or expressing breast milk and have suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection. Subgroups include women infected during pregnancy, acutely ill at the time of delivery, or infected postnatally. The outcomes of interest include suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection in infants, as well as the presence of the virus in breast milk, serum, sweat, or saliva. The guideline development group reviewed evidence from two case reports involving three mother-infant pairs where the mothers had confirmed Zika virus infection during delivery. There was no definitive evidence of Zika virus transmission through breastfeeding, but the limited number of cases resulted in very low-quality evidence. The group acknowledged that new evidence could impact the validity of the guideline's conclusions. The group also considered the values and preferences of mothers regarding breastfeeding in the context of Zika virus infection. Literature on mothers living with HIV, a virus known to be transmissible through breastfeeding, was presented. These studies revealed that mothers weigh complex influences, including feelings of loss, self-blame, and responsibility, when deciding on infant feeding strategies. Social and cultural norms, previous experiences, and advice from healthcare providers also play a role. The group noted that mothers infected with Zika virus, a generally mild and transient infection, may have different preferences compared to those with HIV, a lifelong and largely incurable infection. Clear messaging can reassure mothers and caregivers that while Zika virus has been detected in breast milk, its transmission through breastfeeding is not confirmed, and the potential consequences for the infant remain unknown. The guideline development group emphasized the well-established benefits of breastfeeding, including potential protective effects from antibodies in breast milk against infectious diseases, which may also apply to Zika virus. They noted that the WHO interim recommendations supporting breastfeeding in the context of Zika virus have been well-received in affected countries. Overall, the group found minimal variability in values and preferences regarding breastfeeding in the context of Zika virus infection.
